summary: Introduces the revised Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA) protocol, which lets domain names contain characters from many scripts. This document describes the set of documents that make up the revision and supplies definitions common to all of them. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 3490.

eli5.summary: Domain names used to be mostly plain English letters. This is the table of contents and dictionary for the rules that let names use many alphabets.

subtitle: The vocabulary and road map for the second generation of internationalized domain names, IDNA2008.

tldr.problem: Domain names were limited to ASCII letters, digits and hyphens, and the first version of IDNA left confusion about terms and about how non-ASCII names should be treated.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5890 lists the documents that make up IDNA2008 and defines the shared terms, including LDH labels, A-labels, U-labels and the xn-- prefix, plus the security issues common to the set.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3490 (IDNA2003). It defines terms but does not itself define the lookup or registration procedures.

today: RFC 5890 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2010. It obsoletes RFC 3490 and, according to the unit metadata, updates RFC 4343; the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Introduction to IDNA2008
sections.content:
RFC 5890 is one of a collection of documents that describe a revision of Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA), largely completed in 2008 and known as IDNA2008. The series replaces the earlier version, called IDNA2003 here, which was defined in RFC 3490 and RFC 3491. IDNA2008 keeps the Punycode algorithm (RFC 3492) and the ACE (ASCII-compatible encoding) prefix from the earlier version.

The audience is wider than protocol implementers. The RFC says IDNA must also be understood by people deciding what names are allowed in DNS zone files, what naming policies to use, and how domain name strings are handled in files and systems. The documents are written from the point of view of an IDNA-aware user, application or implementation and do not try to replace a thorough understanding of the DNS.
sections.eli5: People wanted web addresses in their own alphabets. This document introduces the second set of rules for doing that safely and explains the words the rules use.

sections.title: The IDNA2008 Document Set
sections.content:
IDNA2008 is a set of documents, and this one, informally called "Defs", holds the definitions common to all of them. The others are:

  • Rationale (RFC 5894): an overview with explanation and the reasons behind IDNA2008, plus advice for registries and users. It is not normative.
  • Protocol (RFC 5891): the core protocol and its operations. Together with the Bidi document it replaces RFC 3490.
  • Bidi (RFC 5893): special rules for labels with characters written right to left.
  • Tables (RFC 5892): the categories and rules that identify code points allowed in a label, based on Unicode 5.2. It obsoletes RFC 3941 and the IDN use of the tables that RFC refers to.
  • Mapping: guidance on mapping characters to other characters. It is advice and is not a required part of IDNA.
sections.eli5: Think of a set of books. This one is the glossary, another is the main rulebook, one covers languages written right to left, one lists the allowed letters, and one is an optional tips book.

sections.title: Characters and DNS Terms
sections.content:
A code point is an integer in the codespace of a coded character set. In Unicode these run from 0 to 0x10FFFF, and they are written as U+ followed by four to six hexadecimal digits. ASCII means US-ASCII, with 128 characters in the range 0000..007F. Unicode is a superset of ASCII.

On the DNS side the document uses "lookup" for the combination of IDNA operations and what a DNS resolver does, and "registration" for placing an entry in the DNS. Any DNS zone administration is called a "registry". A label is one component of a domain name, so www.example.com has three labels: www, example and com. In these documents "label" means a text label, not a binary or bit-string label.
sections.eli5: A label is one chunk of a web address between the dots. Every letter in every alphabet gets its own number, and these documents use those numbers to talk about letters precisely.

sections.title: LDH Labels and the xn-- Prefix
sections.content:
An LDH label is the classic hostname label: ASCII letters, digits and the hyphen ("letters, digits, hyphen"), with no hyphen at the beginning or end, and no more than 63 octets long. IDNA adds two subsets. Reserved LDH labels (R-LDH) have -- in the third and fourth positions. Non-Reserved LDH labels (NR-LDH) do not.

Only R-LDH labels that begin with xn-- (case independent) can be used by IDNA-aware applications, and these are called XN-labels. If the rest of an XN-label is valid Punycode output and meets the other IDNA tests, it is an A-label. Because of the 63-octet limit, the Punycode part is at most 59 ASCII characters. An XN-label that fails these tests is a Fake A-label. R-LDH labels without the xn-- prefix are not valid IDNA labels and MUST NOT be processed as ordinary LDH labels by IDNA-conforming programs.

A-labels should be produced only in lowercase, since mixed-case annotation never turns out to be useful under the character rules.
sections.eli5: An old-style name is letters, numbers and dashes only. Names in other alphabets get disguised as plain ones that start with "xn--", so older systems can carry them without noticing anything odd.

sections.title: A-labels, U-labels and Equivalence
sections.content:
For IDNA-aware applications there are three valid kinds of label. An A-label is the ASCII-compatible form: xn-- followed by a valid Punycode string, and it must be a complete label. A U-label is a string of Unicode characters in Normalization Form C, with at least one non-ASCII character, in a standard encoding form such as UTF-8. The third kind is the NR-LDH label. Converting between A-label and U-label uses Punycode, adding or removing the ACE prefix.

There is a symmetry constraint: an A-label must be producible by converting a U-label, and that U-label must be producible by converting the A-label. A U-label may expand to up to 252 characters, far over the usual 63-octet limit, because Punycode is so compact. Such labels are valid, but some applications may impose shorter limits.

Labels are equivalent when their A-labels match in a case-independent comparison. A U-label can be compared with another U-label by exact bit-string identity, or converted to an A-label first. IDNA-aware applications allow only A-labels and NR-LDH labels in zone files and queries. U-labels can appear in user interfaces and in protocols that use IDNA forms but do not involve the DNS itself.
sections.eli5: Each foreign-alphabet name has two forms: the pretty version people see (U-label) and the disguised plain version computers pass around (A-label). The rules say the two must always convert back and forth without loss.

sections.title: IDNs, Registries and Domain Name Slots
sections.content:
An internationalized domain name (IDN) is a domain name that contains at least one A-label or U-label and otherwise any mix of NR-LDH labels, A-labels and U-labels. The RFC says registry restrictions on which characters may be registered are mandatory for IDN registries and zones, though the specific restrictions are not part of these specifications. They affect only what can be registered, not lookup, so DNS messages are unchanged.

A domain name slot is a protocol element or function argument explicitly meant to carry a domain name. Examples include the QNAME field of a DNS query, the name argument of getaddrinfo(), and the part of an email address after the at sign. A domain name inside the body text of an email is not in a slot. An IDNA-aware slot is one designated to carry internationalized names. Some protocols cannot carry IDNs, such as the underscore labels used for SRV records.

Characters in a label are numbered in the order they appear on the wire, which matters for scripts written right to left. The RFC also discourages calling anything a "Punycode string" and asks that "Punycode" refer only to the algorithm of RFC 3492.
sections.eli5: A web address that has at least one name-chunk in another alphabet is an IDN. A slot is just a place in a program or message that is supposed to hold a web address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The core worry is that a user typing one internationalized name could be connected to different servers because different software interpreted it differently. IDNA2008 changes the interpretation of a few characters that IDNA2003 mapped to others, so zone administrators should take care. Other issues listed include very long U-labels, which risk buffer overflows and truncation errors, and differing conversions from local character sets to Unicode.

The RFC also covers visually similar characters, for example a Greek omicron mixed with Latin text. It suggests visual indications for names that mix scripts, but notes that there are no comprehensive technical solutions to confusable characters and that simply prohibiting mixed-script labels would not remove the problem. Labels already in the database in the IDNA2003 style, which require its mappings, may be used in name-confusion attacks unless registries are careful.

In some ways testing is stronger, since labels with unassigned code points are now rejected. The documents bypass Stringprep without changing it. The RFC closes by noting that no mechanism based on names alone can stop attacks such as spoofed pages. It specifies no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The big danger is lookalike letters. A name using a Greek letter that looks like an English one could trick you into visiting the wrong site, and nobody has a perfect fix for that.
